article.overview: A dust levitation experiment is an instrument concept for detecting, measuring or imaging fine lunar dust that has been lifted off the surface, mainly by electrostatic forces. Sunlight and the solar wind can electrically charge dust grains, and in some models the finest grains are then pushed into a tenuous cloud above the surface. Faint glows along the lunar horizon, first reported from Surveyor-era imagery, are often linked to this process, but direct in situ confirmation has not been established. Measuring levitated dust would test charging and lofting models and would also inform hazards to optics, mechanisms and crews. The sources reviewed for this article identify no flown instrument dedicated to direct detection of levitated dust; the closest precedents are an Apollo 17 dust-impact experiment and an orbiter dust instrument, and a lander-mounted optical concept is in development [1][2][3][4][7].
article.description: The payload would combine a sensing unit that responds to dust particles with the electronics, timing and environmental monitoring needed to interpret the signal. Two broad approaches have been used or proposed. The first is impact or flux sensing: grains strike a detector, and its response is used to infer speed, direction, kinetic energy or momentum. The Apollo 17 Lunar Ejecta and Meteorites (LEAM) experiment used this approach [4], and the orbital Lunar Dust EXperiment (LDEX) on LADEE measured dust impacts in situ [7]. The second is optical detection: a pulsed light source illuminates the near-surface volume and cameras record scattered light, from which particle positions can be estimated. A DLR concept pairs a pulsed 532 nm laser with a stereo camera system for this purpose [2]. Impact sensors are direct and robust, but they sample only where grains reach the detector. Optical systems can sample a volume, but their performance depends on particle scattering, illumination geometry and camera speed. Because lofting is expected to depend on the solar environment, a useful payload would also need an accurate time reference and records of the illumination geometry [3][4].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main scientific purpose of such a payload is to establish whether electrostatic lofting moves significant amounts of dust, how high grains are lifted, which particle sizes are involved and how often the process occurs. These questions bear on how the lunar surface evolves and how dust is distributed around the Moon. Lunar dust is generated when hypervelocity micrometeoroid impacts strike the surface [5], so measurements of levitated grains would connect impact production with surface transport. Applications include the design of optical and thermal surfaces that must stay clean, protection of mechanisms and seals, assessment of astronaut and equipment exposure, and validation of models used for surface operations. The DLR team identifies optical hazards, mechanical wear, lunar-based astronomy and astronaut health as reasons to measure dust levitation, particularly for Artemis-era and longer-term surface activity [2].
article.operating_principle: Charging comes from the local plasma and from photoemission driven by solar ultraviolet and X-ray radiation [2]. Rosenfeld and Zakharov argue that an isolated fine grain can acquire units to dozens of elementary charges, whereas a grain resting on the surface has an average charge several orders of magnitude lower because the surface charge is patchy. Fluctuating positive and negative spots at the submicron scale can, in their model, lift particles of about 0.1 µm or smaller [1]. The DLR group uses a dynamic fountain model in which charging, lofting and particle motion are linked through the sheath above the surface. In their analysis, only under fast solar streams do 1–10 µm particles gain enough potential to escape the sheath [2]. Laboratory drop experiments in vacuum, with a photoemitting plate standing in for lunar rock, produced negatively charged grains, which supports the charging step [8]. Optical detection works by scattering light from particles, and impact detection converts a grain's arrival into a mechanical or electrical signal. A payload's sensitivity therefore depends on both the physics of charging and the design of its detector.
article.scientific_importance: Observations of a glow along the lunar horizon at sunrise and sunset have been reported since the Surveyor era, and Apollo crews and orbital photographs also recorded bright features near the terminator. The Surveyor glow is commonly attributed to forward scattering of sunlight by fine electrostatically levitated grains, and that interpretation remains widely cited [3]. However, the same observations have competing explanations, and zodiacal light can mask the glow in some datasets [3]. A 2011 Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera test found the horizon glow dimmer than predicted for that geometry, which reinforces the need for direct measurements [3]. LDEX found no evidence for a population of about 0.1 µm grains lofted over the terminator [7], a result in tension with some levitation models. A dedicated payload would therefore have high scientific value because it could discriminate between competing models of surface charging, dust transport and optical glow.

physical_specifications.note: No universal mass, size, power or sensitivity specification exists for a dust levitation experiment. The examples below are a flown lunar surface impact detector, a flown orbital dust instrument and a lander concept. Values are attributed to specific sources, and they are left null where a verified figure was not found.

examples.name: Apollo 17 Lunar Ejecta and Meteorites (LEAM) experiment
examples.mass_note: A secondary summary gives a detector mass of 7.4 kg; no primary value was verified during drafting, so the field is null.
examples.sensor_configuration: Three sensors (east, west, up). The east and up sensors each use pairs of parallel film-grid arrays 5 cm apart, with the rear grid on an acoustic impact plate. The west sensor lacked the front film array and could not measure particle speed.
examples.deployment_geometry: About 7.5 m north-east of the ALSEP central station; east sensor axis at 025 degrees.
examples.operating_phases: First phase of 60 hours of lunar day and 60 hours of lunar night with sensor covers in place; a squib system then removed the covers.
examples.measured_quantities: Speed, direction, kinetic energy and momentum of dust particles, with speed derived from time of flight.
examples.reported_results: Most detected dust was reported as low-energy particles of lunar origin, with no high-energy interstellar candidates. A summary describes a large increase in particle arrivals every morning, which later work links to sunrise-triggered levitation and transport of slow, highly charged dust.
examples.thermal_anomaly: Temperatures exceeded the design rating during the first attempt at a full lunar day. Overheating from 8 July 1976 left only static by 16 July 1976. A Wikipedia summary attributes the temperature rise to charged dust darkening the instrument, citing a 2006 article.

examples.name: LADEE Lunar Dust EXperiment (LDEX)
examples.particle_size_range_um: About 0.1 to 5 (approximately 100 nm to 5 µm), according to conference and press summaries.
examples.reported_results: Persistent, non-spherical and asymmetric dust cloud around the Moon, with highest densities in the 6-8 local-time range, consistent with ejecta from continual impact bombardment. No evidence found for the approximately 0.1 micrometre grains lofted over the terminator that some levitation models require.
examples.qualification: Figures come from conference and press summaries; the primary paper was not opened during drafting.

examples.name: DLR Lunar Levitation Dust Instrument (lander concept)
examples.flight_status: Not flown. Presented at the European Lunar Symposium, June 2025, as a conference talk, not peer-reviewed.
examples.sensor_configuration: Pulsed 532 nm laser paired with a stereo camera system.
examples.laboratory_validation: A 2026 EPSC conference abstract describes a bench test with a 532 nm pulsed laser at a repetition rate of about 100 Hz, aligned with a high-resolution CMOS camera, using silver-coated silica microspheres and copper powder as dust analogues.
examples.unverified_items: Laser pulse energy, camera frame rate, mass, dimensions and power are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed. Pulse-energy values in secondary search summaries could not be verified against the primary paper and are not recorded.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: Dimensions, mass and power are not established for the payload class as a whole. For the flown examples, the sources reviewed do not provide verified figures for the LDEX instrument or for the Apollo 17 LEAM sensor dimensions and power. A secondary summary gives a LEAM detector mass of 7.4 kg, but no primary value was verified during drafting, so mass is recorded as null. The DLR concept has no published dimensions, mass or power in the sources reviewed. Any new payload would need its dimensions set by the measurement range, the required optical baseline and the mounting and thermal constraints.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Not established for the payload class. Recorded values: LEAM null (secondary summary reports 7.4 kg, unverified); LDEX null; DLR concept null.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Not publicly specified in the sources reviewed for any of the three examples.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A payload must operate in a vacuum with strong thermal cycling, intense ultraviolet exposure and a plasma environment that changes with solar conditions. Electronics and optics need thermal control and protection from dust. The LEAM record shows how quickly thermal margins can be exceeded: temperatures went beyond the design rating during the first attempt at a full lunar day, and a Wikipedia summary attributes the temperature rise to charged dust darkening the instrument, citing a 2006 article [4]. Optical instruments need clean, stable windows and a sightline unaffected by the lander's own plume or by dust disturbed during landing. Operations must also consider solar geometry, because the expected levitation signal depends on sunrise and sunset timing [3][4].
article.limitations: A single sensor or a single-point payload can detect grains but may not determine their source region or their full vertical distribution. Impact detectors respond only to particles that reach them, so they may miss grains that never arrive. Optical systems depend on scattering efficiency and detection range, which may be far smaller than the distance over which dust might be lifted. Interpretation depends on charging and lofting models that remain unvalidated in situ, and the Apollo-era data are affected by instrument thermal problems and contested interpretation [4]. Most numerical values in this draft come from secondary summaries and conference material rather than primary datasets.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A dust levitation experiment could be delivered either as a lander-mounted surface payload or as an orbiter instrument. The two classes have different integration, deployment and operating constraints.
transportation_process: Surface payload: integrate with the lander on Earth, launch, transfer towards the Moon and deliver to the surface.
Surface payload: connect power and data interfaces, provide thermal control and mount on a stable, level base with a defined viewing geometry that avoids the lander plume and landing-disturbed dust.
Orbiter payload: integrate with the spacecraft on Earth, launch, transfer through cruise and lunar orbit insertion, commission, then operate under pointing and thermal constraints.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Surface deployment could be by astronaut, by robotic arm or by a passive mounting, as in the Apollo deployment of LEAM [4]. Its measurements would depend on the mounting geometry and the lander's environment. For an orbiter instrument such as LDEX, measurements depend on orbit geometry and local-time coverage, as reflected in the local-time distribution of dust density reported for LDEX [7].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Apollo 17 LEAM was deployed by the astronauts as part of the ALSEP experiment package [4]. LDEX flew on the LADEE orbiter [7].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No lander, rover or orbiter compatibility is asserted in this article. Any compatibility assessment would need mass, dimensions, mounting points, landing loads, power and data interfaces compared with verified spacecraft specifications.

article.historical_significance: Horizon glow was recorded in Surveyor-era images, and Surveyor 6 is cited as the first observation of the glow at the terminator [2][3]. Apollo crews reported bands or rays near sunrise and sunset, and Apollo 15 and 17 coronal photographs showed excessive brightness [3]. The Apollo 17 LEAM experiment operated from 1972 and was shut down in July 1976 after overheating. Its interpretation as levitation remains contested [4]. A 2011 LROC test provided an upper constraint on the glow [3]. LDEX gave the first dedicated orbital measurements of the lunar dust exosphere [7], and the DLR concept of 2025 is the most recent dedicated levitation-instrument proposal in the sources reviewed [2].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: The term 'dust levitation experiment' describes a class of investigations rather than one standard instrument, and the examples above are not interchangeable. The article relies on secondary summaries for several Apollo-era and LDEX values. The primary NASA LEAM document identified during research [6] could not be read during drafting, so the LEAM description rests on the Wikipedia summary [4]. The DLR concept is conference material, not peer-reviewed, and its performance figures come from modelling or bench tests. Charging and lofting models disagree on particle sizes and heights, and the approximately 0.1 µm grains that some models require were not found in LDEX data [7]. The origin of the horizon glow remains contested, with competing explanations including forward scattering by larger grains and transient gases [3]. No verified image assets are included in this version, and no lander or orbiter compatibility has been established.
